title: Methane Explosion at Pakistan Coal Mine Kills 34 as Rescue Teams Search for Survivors
excerpt: A methane blast collapsed two adjacent mines near Quetta at a depth of 4,000 feet, killing workers from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and renewing calls for mine safety reform.
body:
• A methane gas explosion at a coal mining complex in Sorange, near Quetta in Balochistan, killed at least 34 miners on July 30.
  • All 42 workers inside the mine at the time were from Shangla district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province; rescue operations continue for remaining trapped miners.
  • The explosion damaged two adjacent mines at a depth of roughly 4,000 feet, with rescue teams working in dangerous underground conditions.
  • Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti has ordered a detailed investigation as the disaster renews scrutiny of Pakistan's chronic mine safety failures.

The Blast

A powerful methane gas explosion tore through a coal mining complex in the Sorange area, roughly 40 kilometres from Quetta, on Wednesday, killing at least 34 miners and trapping several others underground. Two adjacent mines collapsed in the blast, according to Abdul Ghani Baloch, a senior government mining official in the region.

Qurban Jogezai, the owner of the affected mines, told reporters that methane had accumulated deep inside the shafts before igniting. A total of 42 workers were inside the complex at the time, all of them residents of Shangla district in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province — a pattern common in Balochistan's mining industry, where labourers migrate from other provinces to work in dangerous conditions for low wages.

"Two mines close to each other were damaged in a powerful methane gas explosion."

— Abdul Ghani Baloch, senior government mining official

Rescue Operations

Muhammad Fahad, director of operations for the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA), said a rescue operation was still underway to find the remaining trapped miners. Teams were working at a depth of roughly 4,000 feet, according to Muhammad Atif, chief inspector of mines in the province.

Shoaib Nosherwani, Balochistan's minister for mines and mineral development, told Reuters that 36 people were in the collapsed section at the time of the explosion. The discrepancy with the mine owner's figure of 42 reflects the confusion typical of such disasters in remote areas with limited record-keeping.

A Pattern of Tragedy

The disaster is the latest in a grim series of mining accidents in Balochistan, which is rich in coal and mineral deposits but plagued by inadequate safety standards. Earlier in July, four workers were killed in a separate coal mine collapse near the Meting railway station in Sindh's Thatta district. In January 2026, eleven miners died in a similar methane explosion at a mine near Quetta.

Pakistan's mining sector has long been criticised by safety advocates and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan for irregular inspections, poor ventilation systems, and limited safety monitoring. Workers in Balochistan's coal mines routinely operate without basic protective equipment, and methane detection systems are rare.

India's Stake in Regional Safety

While the disaster is a domestic Pakistani tragedy, it resonates across the border. India's own coal mining sector has faced similar scrutiny over safety standards, and the two countries share challenges around regulating extractive industries in remote regions. For the Indian diaspora, the Sorange explosion is a reminder of the human cost of resource extraction in South Asia — a region where economic pressures often override worker protections.

What's Next

Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti has ordered a detailed investigation into the explosion. Whether that inquiry leads to meaningful regulatory reform remains to be seen — similar promises after past disasters have produced little change. Rescue operations will continue until all missing workers are accounted for.
nri_angle: The disaster highlights shared South Asian challenges in mine safety that resonate with India's own extractive industry struggles.
